results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets within 5 of the LAST-shown example but >5 from the first-shown, minus the rate for targets within 5 of the FIRST-shown but >5 from the last (multi-example sets); the model is order-invariant, so t_observed above null_mean means recency (last example weighted more), below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets within 5 of the LAST-shown example but >5 from the first-shown, minus the rate for targets within 5 of the FIRST-shown but >5 from the last (multi-example sets); the model is order-invariant, so t_observed above null_mean means recency (last example weighted more), below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    first = s[:, 0]
    last = s[np.arange(len(s)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    dl = np.abs(t - last); dfi = np.abs(t - first)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & (dl <= 5) & (dfi > 5)) - rate(base & (dfi <= 5) & (dl > 5))

results.name: set_size_generalization_slope
results.description: OLS slope of the non-example yes rate (per number-of-examples level, 1-4) on the number of examples; t_observed above null_mean (less negative) means generalization tightens less with more examples than the tempered size principle predicts, below means it tightens more.
results.code:
# name: set_size_generalization_slope
# description: OLS slope of the non-example yes rate (per number-of-examples level, 1-4) on the number of examples; t_observed above null_mean (less negative) means generalization tightens less with more examples than the tempered size principle predicts, below means it tightens more.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    base = ~is_ex
    xs = []; ys = []
    for k in range(1, 5):
        m = base & (n == k)
        if m.sum() > 0:
            xs.append(k); ys.append(r[m].mean())
    if len(xs) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.polyfit(np.array(xs, float), np.array(ys), 1)[0])

results.name: mult5_set_mult5_target_gap
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 5, yes rate for non-example multiple-of-5 targets minus for non-multiple-of-5 targets; t_observed above null_mean means people use the "multiples of 5/10" rule more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: mult5_set_mult5_target_gap
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 5, yes rate for non-example multiple-of-5 targets minus for non-multiple-of-5 targets; t_observed above null_mean means people use the "multiples of 5/10" rule more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    all5 = np.where(v, s % 5 == 0, True).all(axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & all5 & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & (t % 5 == 0)) - rate(base & (t % 5 != 0))

results.name: odd_set_far_odd_yes_rate
results.description: In all-odd sets (>=2 examples), yes rate for odd non-example targets >10 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example; t_observed above null_mean means people generalize the "odd numbers" rule more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: odd_set_far_odd_yes_rate
# description: In all-odd sets (>=2 examples), yes rate for odd non-example targets >10 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example; t_observed above null_mean means people generalize the "odd numbers" rule more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    par = np.where(v, s % 2, np.nan)
    allodd = np.nanmin(par, axis=1) == 1
    ld = (np.where(v, s % 10, -1) == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & allodd & ~is_ex & (t % 2 == 1) & (d > 10) & ~ld
    return rate(m)

results.name: extrapolation_above_minus_below
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets above the largest example minus for targets below the smallest example (multi-example sets); t_observed above null_mean means people extrapolate upward more readily than the model (a magnitude/direction asymmetry), below means downward more.
results.code:
# name: extrapolation_above_minus_below
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets above the largest example minus for targets below the smallest example (multi-example sets); t_observed above null_mean means people extrapolate upward more readily than the model (a magnitude/direction asymmetry), below means downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    mx = np.nanmax(sv, axis=1); mn = np.nanmin(sv, axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & (t > mx)) - rate(base & (t < mn))

results.name: prime_set_prime_vs_oddnonprime_gap
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all primes, yes rate for prime non-example targets minus for odd non-prime targets; t_observed above null_mean means people use the "primes" rule more than the model, below means less (they treat such sets as merely odd/near).
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_vs_oddnonprime_gap
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all primes, yes rate for prime non-example targets minus for odd non-prime targets; t_observed above null_mean means people use the "primes" rule more than the model, below means less (they treat such sets as merely odd/near).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    pr = np.zeros(102, dtype=bool)
    for k in range(2, 101):
        pr[k] = all(k % a for a in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1))
    si = np.where(v, s, 0).astype(int)
    allp = np.where(v, pr[si], True).all(axis=1)
    ti = t.astype(int)
    base = (n >= 2) & allp & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & pr[ti]) - rate(base & ~pr[ti] & (ti % 2 == 1))

results.name: single_example_far_parity_gap
results.description: In single-example sets, yes rate for targets >10 from the example with the same parity minus with the opposite parity; t_observed above null_mean means one example triggers parity generalization more than the model predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: single_example_far_parity_gap
# description: In single-example sets, yes rate for targets >10 from the example with the same parity minus with the opposite parity; t_observed above null_mean means one example triggers parity generalization more than the model predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    base = (n == 1) & ~is_ex & (d > 10)
    sp = (t % 2) == (s[:, 0] % 2)
    return rate(base & sp) - rate(base & ~sp)

results.name: square_set_square_target_yes_rate
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all perfect squares, yes rate for non-example perfect-square targets; t_observed above null_mean means people generalize the "squares" rule more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: square_set_square_target_yes_rate
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all perfect squares, yes rate for non-example perfect-square targets; t_observed above null_mean means people generalize the "squares" rule more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    v = ~np.isnan(s); n = v.sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    sv = np.where(v, s, np.nan)
    is_ex = (np.where(v, s, -999) == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(sv - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    sq = np.zeros(102, dtype=bool); sq[[k * k for k in range(1, 11)]] = True
    si = np.where(v, s, 0).astype(int)
    allsq = np.where(v, sq[si], True).all(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & allsq & ~is_ex & sq[t.astype(int)]
    return rate(m)
